Q01.question: How would you describe current adoption of robotic surgery in your market?

France.answer: Adoption is growing, but it remains concentrated in larger academic hospitals and private centres with stronger capital budgets, while smaller regional hospitals are much slower.

evidence.quote: Adoption is growing, but it is still concentrated in larger academic hospitals and private centres with stronger capital budgets. Smaller regional hospitals are much slower.

Germany.answer: Adoption is growing, but it is quite uneven with large university hospitals being much more advanced while many smaller hospitals are still waiting.

evidence.quote: It is growing, but adoption is quite uneven. Large university hospitals are much more advanced, while many smaller hospitals are still waiting.

United Kingdom.answer: Adoption is increasing, and in some larger NHS trusts robotic surgery is becoming standard for selected procedures, though access still varies significantly by hospital.

evidence.quote: Adoption is increasing, and in some larger NHS trusts robotic surgery is becoming standard for selected procedures. But access still varies significantly by hospital.

Q02.question: What are the main barriers to adoption?

France.answer: The main barriers to adoption include capital budget approval, the need for a strong economic case addressing utilisation, procedure volume, and maintenance costs, ensuring multiple surgeons are trained to maintain high utilisation, and limited budgets in smaller regional hospitals.

evidence.quote: The biggest issue is still capital budget approval. Hospitals may like the technology clinically, but purchasing committees need a strong economic case before approving a system.

Very important. The clinical argument may get surgeons interested, but the finance team wants to understand utilisation, procedure volume, maintenance cost and whether the system will actually pay for itself.
Training matters, especially in the first year. If only one surgeon can use the system, the economics become difficult. Hospitals want several surgeons trained so utilisation is high enough.
Adoption is growing, but it is still concentrated in larger academic hospitals and private centres with stronger capital budgets. Smaller regional hospitals are much slower.

Germany.answer: The main barriers to adoption are high costs and capital purchase pressures, the need to prove sufficient system utilisation, and uneven adoption where smaller hospitals lag behind large university hospitals.

evidence.quote: Cost is the first barrier. These are large capital purchases, and hospital finances are under pressure. The second issue is proving that the system will be used enough.
Very important operationally. If the hospital buys a system but only one surgeon is comfortable using it, utilisation will be poor. That weakens the business case.
It is growing, but adoption is quite uneven. Large university hospitals are much more advanced, while many smaller hospitals are still waiting.

United Kingdom.answer: The main barriers to adoption include funding constraints, capital cycle delays, and limitations in training capacity for surgeons and theatre staff.

evidence.quote: Funding is important, but I would say training capacity is just as important. You can buy a system, but if you cannot train enough surgeons and theatre staff, adoption stalls.
Around six to nine months can happen if funding is already available. If the trust has to wait for a new capital cycle, it can take much longer.

Q03.question: How important are hospital budgets and ROI in purchasing decisions?

France.answer: Hospital budgets and economics are very important in purchasing decisions. While clinical arguments and outcomes are necessary, finance teams and purchasing committees require a strong economic case, capital budget approval, and proof of utilisation, maintenance costs, and whether the system will pay for itself.

evidence.quote: Very important. The clinical argument may get surgeons interested, but the finance team wants to understand utilisation, procedure volume, maintenance cost and whether the system will actually pay for itself.
Clinical outcomes are necessary, but they are not enough on their own. If two systems offer similar outcomes, the hospital will look hard at economics and utilisation.
The biggest issue is still capital budget approval. Hospitals may like the technology clinically, but purchasing committees need a strong economic case before approving a system.

Germany.answer: Cost is the primary barrier for these large capital purchases because hospital finances are under pressure. The economic case, total cost of ownership, expected procedure volume, maintenance, and service contracts ultimately decide whether a purchase gets approved.

evidence.quote: We look at total cost of ownership, expected procedure volume, maintenance, service contracts and training requirements. A strong clinical case helps, but the economic case decides whether it gets approved.
Cost is the first barrier. These are large capital purchases, and hospital finances are under pressure. The second issue is proving that the system will be used enough.

United Kingdom.answer: Economics matter in purchasing decisions, but the discussion is not purely financial. Economics and clinical strategy are balanced, and hospitals also evaluate patient outcomes, length of stay, surgeon recruitment, and clinical position alongside financial sustainability.

evidence.quote: I would say economics and clinical strategy are balanced. I would not say finance alone decides the purchase.

It matters, but the discussion is not always purely financial. Hospitals also consider patient outcomes, length of stay, surgeon recruitment and whether the technology improves their clinical position.

Q04.question: How important are surgeon training and clinical outcomes?

France.answer: Surgeon training is important, especially in the first year to ensure high utilisation, and clinical outcomes are necessary (though not enough on their own if systems offer similar outcomes).

evidence.quote: Clinical outcomes are necessary, but they are not enough on their own. If two systems offer similar outcomes, the hospital will look hard at economics and utilisation.

Very important. The clinical argument may get surgeons interested, but the finance team wants to understand utilisation, procedure volume, maintenance cost and whether the system will actually pay for itself.
Training matters, especially in the first year. If only one surgeon can use the system, the economics become difficult. Hospitals want several surgeons trained so utilisation is high enough.

Germany.answer: Training requirements are considered operationally important because having only one surgeon comfortable using the system leads to poor utilisation and weakens the business case, while a strong clinical case helps support overall approval alongside economics.

evidence.quote: We look at total cost of ownership, expected procedure volume, maintenance, service contracts and training requirements. A strong clinical case helps, but the economic case decides whether it gets approved.
Very important operationally. If the hospital buys a system but only one surgeon is comfortable using it, utilisation will be poor. That weakens the business case.

United Kingdom.answer: Training capacity is considered just as important as funding because adoption stalls if enough surgeons and theatre staff cannot be trained, and patient outcomes are part of what hospitals consider.

evidence.quote: Funding is important, but I would say training capacity is just as important. You can buy a system, but if you cannot train enough surgeons and theatre staff, adoption stalls.

It matters, but the discussion is not always purely financial. Hospitals also consider patient outcomes, length of stay, surgeon recruitment and whether the technology improves their clinical position.

Q05.question: What adoption trend do you expect over the next 3–5 years?

France.answer: Adoption is expected to continue increasing steadily rather than explosively, with perhaps 15 to 20 percent more procedures annually in stronger centres, while smaller hospitals remain slower.

evidence.quote: I expect adoption to continue increasing, probably steadily rather than explosively. I would expect maybe 15 to 20 percent more procedures annually in some of the stronger centres, but smaller hospitals will remain slower.

Germany.answer: Growth is expected to be gradual rather than a dramatic jump, with continued procedure volume growth closer to high single digits or low double digits rather than 20 percent across the whole market.

evidence.quote: Yes, but I would not expect a dramatic jump. I think growth will be gradual, especially because many hospitals have other competing capital priorities.
I would expect continued growth, but probably closer to high single digits or low double digits in procedure volumes rather than something like 20 percent across the whole market.

United Kingdom.answer: Adoption could accelerate if training expands and systems become more cost competitive, with procedure growth potentially above 15 percent annually in some areas.

evidence.quote: I am quite positive. I think adoption could accelerate if training expands and systems become more cost competitive. I could see procedure growth above 15 percent annually in some areas.

Q06.question: What is the typical hospital decision-making timeline for purchasing a new robotic system?

France.answer: The typical timeline is six to twelve months once the hospital is serious, though it can take longer if the capital committee delays the purchase into the next budget cycle.

evidence.quote: Six to twelve months is realistic once the hospital becomes serious. It can be longer if the capital committee pushes the purchase into the next budget cycle.

Germany.answer: A timeline of nine to eighteen months is common as procurement, clinical leadership, finance, and management need to align.

evidence.quote: Nine to eighteen months is common. Procurement, clinical leadership, finance and management all need to align, so it can move slowly.

United Kingdom.answer: A timeline of around six to nine months can occur if funding is already available, but it can take much longer if the trust must wait for a new capital cycle.

evidence.quote: Around six to nine months can happen if funding is already available. If the trust has to wait for a new capital cycle, it can take much longer.
